world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Dza is a tonal language and tone plays a function in lexical and grammatical contrast. So far, three contrastive level tonesː H, M and L are clearly attested. Furthermore, there are three contour tonesː HL, LH and LHL. [Othaniel 2020: 29] ... Typically, words are monosyllabic in Dza. Verb forms, apart from phrasal verbs, are either [V], [CV] or [CVC]. However, in the case of nouns, the above syllable types can combine to form two syllables, three syllables and four syllable words. [Othaniel 2022: 21]
new_statements.citation: Othaniel, Nlabephee Kefas. 2020. Verbal morphosyntax in Dza, an Adamawa language of Taraba State. MA thesis, Theological College of Northern Nigeria, Bukuru / University of Jos, §3.1.3 Lexical and grammatical tone; supplemented by Othaniel, Nlabephee Kefas. 2022. A phonetic study of breathy voicing in Dza. MA2 thesis, Université Paris Cité, §3.4.4
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages are verbatim at the stated locators. Othaniel 2020 (Verbal morphosyntax in Dza),, PDF p. 41 = printed p. 29, §3.1.3 'Lexical and Grammatical Tone': "Dza is a tonal language and tone plays a function in lexical and grammatical contrast. So far, three contrastive level tonesː H, M and L are clearly attested. Furthermore, there are three contour tonesː HL, LH and LHL." followed by Table 3.10 (H/M/L/LH minimal sets ta/ku) and the grammatical-tone examples (6) i-vi (interrogative, object vs possessive pronoun, NEG.HAB, locative nominals). Othaniel 2022 (breathy voicing MA2), PDF p. 21, §3.4.4 'Syllable types and word structures in Dza': "Typically, words are monosyllabic in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated by any source. Dza is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) and contour tones (HL, LH, LHL; Benson also lists M-contours), tone carrying both lexical and grammatical contrasts (mood, object vs possessive pronoun, aspect in negation, locative nominals); vowel length is non-contrastive; words are typically monosyllabic. None of the seven accessible descriptions uses the words stress or accent for Dza.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement to have exceptions). Benson 2020: 340 notes vowel lengthening of the ideophone tūtū for emphasis, an expressive device, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone description from a native-speaker linguist's MA theses (phonology chapter of a morphosyntax thesis; background chapter of a phonetics thesis), based on citation forms and example sentences. Tone marking follows the author's own 2014/2016 phonology write-ups, which are unpublished. The statement is about tone only; silence on stress is an absence in the sources, not an explicit 'no stress' claim.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Dza / Dzə (exonym Jenjo, Jen), ISO jen, Glottolog dzaa1238, spoken along the northern Benue bank; Othaniel 2022 §3.2 and AdaGram name three dialects (Nwabang, Dzakah, Ye) converging on one variety, with no separate glottocodes; Kleinewillinghöfer's wordlist is 'Dza (aka Jen) of Kaigama'. Tha (Joole Manga) and Doso are treated as distinct languages of the same cluster, not as Dza.

sources.citation: AdaGram project (LLACAN-CNRS), Dza language page, https://llacan.cnrs.fr/AdaGram/accessed 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Language background (three dialects Nwabang, Dzakah, Ye; ~100,000 ethnic Dza, fewer speakers), full Dza bibliography, and the open PDFs of Othaniel 2017/2020/2022 and Kleinewillinghöfer 2015; states Othaniel is now writing an ELDP-funded PhD thesis on Dza. Nothing on stress.

Secondary: 'Like most West African languages, Dza is a tonal language' with five tonemes (H, M, L, rising, falling), tone unmarked in orthography; no stress statement. Its citation to Othaniel 2020 on the LLACAN site is how the primary PDFs were located.
